package_info.package_versions: Varies (see individual threats: Mal.Metrica - WordPress plugins, Wpeeper - repackaged Android apps, GoldDigger/GoldFamily - Android/iOS apps, DarkGate - Windows binaries)
package_info.why_malicious: These packages and binaries are malicious because they inject deceptive scripts, establish covert command-and-control channels, exfiltrate sensitive biometric and identification data, and enable full remote access and data theft. They exploit legitimate platforms (WordPress, Android, iOS, Windows) to compromise users, evade detection, and facilitate monetization, identity theft, and further attacks.

execution_context.trigger: runtime (when a WordPress site is loaded or visited by a user)
execution_context.file_location: Injected into legitimate WordPress plugin files (e.g., tagDiv Composer, Popup Builder, WP Go Maps, Beautiful Cookie Consent Banner)
required_permissions: network (to load external scripts and perform redirections)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Injected JavaScript that loads a Yandex.Metrica analytics script, displays a fake CAPTCHA prompt to the user, and upon user interaction, redirects the browser to attacker-controlled malicious domains.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime (when a user visits the infected WordPress site), the code injects a Yandex.Metrica script into the page, displays a deceptive CAPTCHA prompt, and upon user interaction, redirects the user to a malicious domain, resulting in click fraud and potential malware delivery.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code is injected into unrelated plugin files and performs user deception by displaying a fake CAPTCHA and redirecting users to known malicious domains, which is not part of legitimate plugin functionality.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate WordPress plugins should not inject third-party analytics scripts in this manner, nor should they display deceptive prompts or redirect users to untrusted external domains without user consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate plugins may use analytics scripts or CAPTCHA prompts, but these are implemented transparently, with user consent, and never redirect users to malicious sites.
key_indicators: Presence of Yandex.Metrica script injected into unrelated plugin files
Display of a fake CAPTCHA prompt not associated with plugin features
Redirection to domains known for malicious activity
Modification of plugin files outside of normal update processes

execution_context.trigger: runtime (Android app execution after installation, especially in repackaged apps from unofficial sources)
execution_context.file_location: Malicious code embedded in repackaged Android app code (Wpeeper Trojan)
required_permissions: device_admin (to maintain persistence and evade removal)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Malicious code within repackaged Android apps that establishes command-and-control (C2) communication by routing traffic through compromised WordPress relay servers, enabling remote attacker control and evasion of detection.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime (after installation and app launch), the code establishes covert C2 communication by sending encrypted traffic through hacked WordPress sites acting as relays, allowing remote attackers to issue commands, control the device, and evade detection by security tools.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The use of compromised WordPress sites as C2 relays is a known evasion technique, and the code is present in repackaged apps distributed outside official app stores, increasing the risk of undetected compromise.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate Android apps should not communicate with unknown or compromised servers, nor should they establish covert C2 channels or request excessive permissions unrelated to their stated functionality.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate apps use background network communication, but only with trusted servers and with clear user consent; they do not use compromised third-party infrastructure for C2.
key_indicators: C2 traffic routed through hacked WordPress sites
Presence of malicious code in repackaged APKs from unofficial sources
Requests for excessive permissions (device admin, background execution)
Encrypted or obfuscated network traffic to untrusted domains
Attempts to evade antivirus and security detection

execution_context.trigger: runtime (Android/iOS app execution after installation, especially during onboarding or authentication steps)
execution_context.file_location: GoldDigger/GoldFamily trojan code embedded in mobile app binaries
required_permissions: filesystem (to store and access captured data)
biometric_data (to access device biometric sensors and data)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Malicious code that captures facial recognition data and personal identification documents (such as ID cards or passports) using the device camera and biometric sensors, then exfiltrates this sensitive information to attacker-controlled servers. In some cases, the code also generates AI-based deepfake images for further social engineering.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime (when the app is executed and prompts for biometric or document capture), the code collects facial recognition data and personal identification documents via the device camera and sensors, then transmits this sensitive data to attacker-controlled infrastructure, enabling identity theft and unauthorized account access.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The unsolicited collection and exfiltration of biometric and identification data is highly sensitive and not required for most legitimate app functions, especially without explicit user consent or clear purpose.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate apps should only collect biometric or identification data with explicit user consent, for a clear and disclosed purpose, and must securely handle and store such data without unauthorized transmission.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some banking or authentication apps may collect such data, but only with strong user consent, secure storage, and transparent privacy policies; they do not exfiltrate data to unknown servers.
key_indicators: Unsolicited access to camera and biometric sensors
Exfiltration of facial recognition and document images to unknown servers
Use of AI-generated deepfake images for social engineering
Absence of user consent or privacy disclosures
Network traffic containing biometric or document data

execution_context.trigger: runtime (Windows system, after execution of the DarkGate RAT binary)
execution_context.file_location: DarkGate RAT binary (Borland Delphi executable, typically dropped in user or temp directories)
required_permissions: filesystem (to read/write files and steal data)
network (for C2 communication and data exfiltration)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Code within the DarkGate RAT binary that performs process injection into legitimate processes, downloads and executes additional payloads, steals sensitive data (such as credentials and files), executes arbitrary shell commands, and logs keystrokes, providing full remote access to the attacker. The code also attempts to bypass Microsoft Defender SmartScreen.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime (after the RAT binary is executed on a Windows system), the code injects itself into legitimate processes, downloads and executes additional payloads, steals sensitive data, executes arbitrary shell commands, and logs keystrokes, resulting in full remote access and data theft for the attacker.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The combination of process injection, keylogging, remote shell command execution, and attempts to bypass security controls is characteristic of advanced RATs and is not found in legitimate software.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal applications do not inject into other processes, log keystrokes, execute arbitrary shell commands, or attempt to bypass security features like Microsoft Defender SmartScreen.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some remote administration tools may have similar features, but only with explicit user consent, transparent operation, and legitimate distribution channels; they are not covertly installed or distributed via malware campaigns.
key_indicators: Process injection into legitimate Windows processes
Bypassing or disabling Microsoft Defender SmartScreen
Downloading and executing additional payloads from attacker infrastructure

attack_chain.action: Initial infection via exploitation of vulnerable WordPress plugins, installation of repackaged Android/iOS apps, or execution of malicious Windows binaries (Mal.Metrica, Wpeeper, GoldDigger/GoldFamily, DarkGate).
attack_chain.leads_to: Establishment of persistence mechanisms and setup for command-and-control communication.

attack_chain.action: Establish command-and-control channels using hacked WordPress sites, attacker-controlled infrastructure, or covert cloud services to enable remote attacker control.
attack_chain.leads_to: Remote attacker access to compromised systems and ability to issue commands or exfiltrate data.

attack_chain.action: User deception and sensitive data collection through fake CAPTCHA prompts, biometric capture, document theft, and keylogging.
attack_chain.leads_to: Exfiltration of sensitive user data and further compromise of user accounts or systems.

attack_chain.action: Exfiltration of collected sensitive data (credentials, biometric data, documents, keystrokes) to attacker-controlled infrastructure for monetization, identity theft, or further attacks.
attack_chain.leads_to: Monetization, identity theft, lateral movement, or launching of additional attacks.

behavioral_signatures: Unexpected injection of third-party analytics scripts (e.g., Yandex.Metrica) into WordPress plugin files
Display of fake CAPTCHA prompts and subsequent user redirection to untrusted or malicious domains
Android/iOS apps establishing network connections to hacked WordPress sites or unknown servers
Unsolicited collection and exfiltration of biometric or identification data from mobile devices
Process injection, keylogging, and remote shell command execution by user-space binaries on Windows systems
Attempts to bypass or disable Microsoft Defender SmartScreen or other security controls
file_indicators: Modified WordPress plugin files containing injected JavaScript referencing Yandex.Metrica
Repackaged Android APKs with additional or excessive permissions (network, device admin, background execution)
Presence of GoldDigger/GoldFamily or DarkGate binaries in user or temporary directories
Unexpected changes or access to biometric data storage or access logs on mobile devices
Executable files with process injection and keylogging capabilities
network_indicators: Outbound connections to Yandex.Metrica domains from unrelated WordPress plugins
Network traffic to known malicious or compromised WordPress domains used as C2 relays
Encrypted or obfuscated C2 traffic to attacker infrastructure, including cloud services (e.g., OneDrive) and hacked WordPress sites
Exfiltration of biometric or document data to unknown or untrusted endpoints
Unusual network activity from mobile apps or binaries not present in official app stores
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for unauthorized modifications to WordPress plugin files and unexpected third-party script injections. Analyze network traffic for connections to known malicious domains, hacked WordPress sites, or cloud-based C2 infrastructure. Use mobile app analysis tools to detect repackaged apps with excessive permissions or suspicious network behavior. Employ endpoint detection and response (EDR) solutions to identify process injection, keylogging, and remote command execution. Flag apps or binaries that access or transmit biometric data without clear user consent or legitimate business need. Correlate file, network, and behavioral indicators to identify multi-stage attack chains.
